issues.legal_issue: The statutory preservation and settlement of a building applies to a person who lawfully held it, not merely to whoever physically possessed it when the estate vested.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a building within an estate subject to statutory vesting and settlement.

The respondents had held the building and its site as tenants, while the appellants claimed the benefit of settlement based on their physical possession after entering the site and demolishing the respondents’ buildings.
issues.conclusion: The word “held” in Section 9 means lawfully held; mere physical possession, including possession by a trespasser, is insufficient to obtain the statutory benefit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 6 and 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act distinguish the estate’s vesting in the State from the subsequent deemed settlement of specified buildings and lands. In context, “held” denotes possession by legal title, not bare possession. The Court relied on Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank Ltd. concerning vesting, Shivashankar Prasad Shah v. Vaikunth Nath Singh concerning similar vesting provisions, K.K. Handique v. The Member, Board of Agricultural Income Tax, Assam on the meaning of “holds,” and Eramma v. Verrupanna on the meaning of “possessed.” It accepted the interpretation in Pheku Chamar v. Harish Chandra.

rule.if: building_settlement_proceeding and building_within_vested_estate and person_physically_possessed_building and not person_had_legal_title_to_hold_building

predicates.building_settlement_proceeding: The dispute arose in a proceeding about who was entitled to a building affected by estate vesting and statutory settlement.
predicates.building_within_vested_estate: The building was situated within an estate that vested in the State.
predicates.person_physically_possessed_building: The person claiming the benefit was physically possessing the building at the relevant time.
predicates.person_had_legal_title_to_hold_building: The person claiming the benefit had a legal title to hold the building.

issues.definition: When a building settlement proceeding concerns a building in a vested estate, physical possession without legal title does not qualify the possessor for settlement.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary absence from a building does not end the lawful holder’s possession where the holder did not voluntarily abandon it, and an unlawful occupier does not gain rights by demolishing the building and replacing it with another structure.
material_facts: The respondents’ family had held the site and residential buildings for many years as tenants.
The respondents left temporarily during communal disturbances for safety and returned when conditions improved; they had not voluntarily abandoned the buildings.
During their absence, the appellants occupied the site, demolished the residential buildings and built a cowshed there.
The Court found that the new structure was a substitution for the demolished buildings and that the respondents were the owners of the building when vesting occurred.
issues.conclusion: The respondents remained the lawful holders and owners of the building at vesting and were entitled to recover both the site and the replacement building; the appellants’ trespass and construction gave them no rights.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 9, the persons lawfully holding a building at vesting retain the benefit of its deemed settlement. Temporary absence for safety is not abandonment where possession was not voluntarily given up. An unlawful trespasser’s demolition and replacement construction does not enhance the trespasser’s rights; on the facts, the replacement structure was treated as a substitution for the former building.

rule.if: recovery_proceeding_after_statutory_vesting and claimant_lawfully_held_building and claimant_absence_was_temporary and claimant_did_not_abandon_building and opposing_party_entered_unlawfully and opposing_party_replaced_demolished_building

predicates.recovery_proceeding_after_statutory_vest: The claimant sought recovery of a site and building after a statutory vesting event.
predicates.claimant_lawfully_held_building: The claimant lawfully held the building before the disputed occupation.
predicates.claimant_absence_was_temporary: The claimant left the building temporarily for safety and later returned.
predicates.claimant_did_not_abandon_building: The claimant did not voluntarily give up possession of the building.
predicates.opposing_party_entered_unlawfully: The opposing party entered and occupied the site without a lawful right to do so.
predicates.opposing_party_replaced_demolished_build: The opposing party demolished the claimant’s building and erected a replacement structure on the site.

issues.definition: When a lawful holder temporarily leaves without abandoning a building and an unlawful occupier replaces it after demolition, the holder may recover the site and replacement building in a recovery proceeding after vesting.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court bench that disagrees with a decision of a coordinate bench of that court should refer the question to a larger bench rather than decline to follow the earlier decision.
material_facts: One division bench of the High Court held that the relevant statutory settlement was limited to buildings lawfully held.
A later division bench declined to follow that decision and reached the contrary interpretation.
The Supreme Court stated that the later bench should have referred the question to a larger bench.
issues.conclusion: Judicial propriety requires a coordinate bench unable to agree with an earlier coordinate-bench decision to refer the question to a larger bench.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule of judicial propriety that a bench of a High Court should not sit in judgment on the correctness of a decision of a coordinate bench; disagreement should be resolved by reference to a larger bench. The Court discussed Pheku Chamar v. Harish Chandra and Bharat v. Ch. Khazan Singh in applying that principle.

predicates.coordinate_bench_case: The matter is before a bench of a court considering a question previously decided by a bench of that same court.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_bench_decision_exists: A coordinate bench of the same court has already decided the question.
predicates.later_bench_disagrees_with_earlier_decis: The later bench cannot agree with the earlier coordinate bench’s decision.

issues.definition: When a later coordinate bench disagrees with an earlier coordinate-bench decision, it must refer the question to a larger bench.
